note: The incidents the fleetops skill grew from. Read by lua/core/lessons.lua once, by id, into the node's own lessons store; never injected into a session. Symptom, cause, fix, rule - a lesson without a rule is an anecdote.

incidents.symptom: Two nodes (nextcloud, mail) went offline for 18.5 hours after fleet control 'did not work' from the laptop agent. The rendezvous itself was up and answering.
incidents.cause: The agent added itself to WASM_AGENT_NETWORK_ADMINS in the wa-rendezvous drop-in (/etc/systemd/system/wa-rendezvous.service.d/managed.conf) and restarted wa-rendezvous to gain control. Peers pin the admin set they were bound with, so they were detached from the directory by the change, not by an outage.
incidents.fix: Restore the admin set and the service file, restart nothing else, let the pinned peers re-register. Then give the node control through the mesh instead: wa fleet push-roster <node>.
incidents.rule: Never edit WASM_AGENT_NETWORK_ADMINS or a wa-rendezvous drop-in to gain control, and never restart wa-rendezvous to apply it. Peers pin the set; use mesh (wa fleet push-roster).

incidents.symptom: The same class of outage again: nodes detached from the rendezvous for about an hour, in the middle of a working fleet.
incidents.cause: The same 'fix' was reached for twice: the control plane was treated as a local setting to edit rather than a shared directory every node pins. The diagnosis step (read last_seen and the operator route) was skipped, so the change was debugging by mutation.
incidents.fix: Read the fleet first (fleetview/nodes: online, last_seen, operator_of_peer), then the rendezvous journal. Push the roster if the goal is control; change nothing in the directory.
incidents.rule: Diagnose before touching shared control plane: fleetview/nodes and the rendezvous journal first, then mesh push-roster. A second occurrence of an incident means the rule was not written down - write it.

incidents.symptom: A Rust rebuild ran for about 40 minutes in a 2-core container, blocking the task, and was still not finished when the agent gave up on it.
incidents.cause: The capacity of the box was never checked before choosing to build there: the build was started assuming a workstation-class machine, and a 2-core container was asked for a full workspace release build.
incidents.fix: Check the cheapest facts first (cores, memory, disk, existing target dir) and choose: an incremental test build of the one crate, or hand the build to a machine that has the capacity. Long builds belong in a managed operation.
incidents.rule: Cheapest check first: read cores/memory/disk before starting a heavy build, build only the crate you touched, and never treat a slow box as a broken build.

incidents.symptom: A cargo build was backgrounded inside one bash call; the call returned, the build's fate was unknown, and the work had to be rediscovered.
incidents.cause: A long-running child was detached instead of supervised. The command's exit status described the shell, not the build, so 'it ran' and 'it worked' were confused.
incidents.fix: Run long work as a managed operation (or a supervised job) whose state can be read back, and verify the artifact (binary path, version, test output), not the launch.
incidents.rule: Long work goes into an operation that outlives the call; verify the effect, not the command. Never background a build inside a single call and walk away.

incidents.symptom: work, mail and nextcloud left the directory within a minute of each other while the rendezvous was up and answering; each binding was accepted and permanent, yet work could not reach any peer and a call to it hung on the relay.
incidents.cause: The same edit a third time: 86a8cbb2 (work) was appended to WASM_AGENT_NETWORK_ADMINS in the wa-rendezvous drop-in and the service restarted (sudo log, 12:41-12:43 local). Every guest's attach tick compared the service's operator list with the set it had consented to and failed on any difference, so a config edit detached a healthy fleet.
incidents.fix: Restore the pinned set and restart only the rendezvous; guests attach on their next tick, without a restart. The class is now patched in lua/core/binding.lua: the tick records the relation (same/added/removed/changed) instead of detaching, admission checks the caller's own vouch per call, and an unreadable service is named binding_service_unavailable. Proof: scripts/test-binding-authority.lua.
incidents.rule: An operator list is a consent record, not a permission gate: attach is reachability, admission is per caller. Never let a directory setting decide whether a node is reachable.

incidents.symptom: With the roster installed and mesh enabled, a peer call became worse than before: openclaw -> mail answered 'mesh call from=2b941f3d to=f6195be1 levels=1->2 verb=read decision=deny reason=unreachable:read_failed:Connection reset by peer (os error 104) transport=relay', and the call failed instead of falling back to the pins it used before. work -> mail stayed remote_refused, and a push-roster from openclaw to work was denied with reason=hierarchy_denied (openclaw level 1 calling up to work level 0).
incidents.cause: Two measured limits, not one. (1) No node has a roster address (all addresses: []), so every mesh call uses the relay hop, and that hop resets the connection for a caller with no binding (openclaw is an unbound host); a mesh denial is an answer, so the caller no longer falls back to pins. (2) The roster hierarchy is strict: a level-1 node cannot call a level-0 node, so openclaw cannot reach work or wasm_the_first.
incidents.fix: Revert mesh.enabled on openclaw (pinned calls work again) and keep the guests' installed roster: it is inert while no mesh call is made. To finish the direct/mesh path: either give the roster real host:port addresses and re-sign it with the fleet private key (not present on work, openclaw or wasm_the_first), or fix the relay's mesh hop to accept an unbound caller, and set every master to level 0 in a re-signed roster for master<->master.
incidents.rule: Enabling mesh on a fleet whose roster has no addresses can reduce reach: a mesh denial does not fall back to pins. Prove a mesh call between two real nodes before enabling it fleet-wide, and treat 'all addresses empty' as 'relay only'.
